title: Species-Identity Ablation: Quantifying How Much 'Trait Prediction' Is Species Recognition
motivation: With TRY species-mean labels, a CNN can score well by recognizing species rather than reading morphology. We need a controlled decomposition of how much predictive signal is species identity versus within-species visual variation.
hypothesis: A model trained with species labels only (no trait labels) will achieve R^2 within ~0.05 of a trait-trained model on held-out species-mean traits, implying most apparent trait signal is species-identity-mediated.
method: Train three models: (a) trait regression, (b) species classification then map class->mean trait (label-free trait transfer), (c) trait regression with species-identity adversarial head. Compare on seen-species and unseen-species splits. Decompose variance via a species-mean oracle baseline.
data: iNaturalist/GBIF images + TRY species means; PlantTraits2024 if available.
baseline: Standard trait-regression CNN (ResNet/ViT) as in 2021 Sci Rep.
metric: R^2 and MAE on seen vs unseen species; fraction of trait variance explained by species-mean oracle.
expected_effect: Species-classification-only model reaches >=80% of trait model R^2 on seen species; gap collapses on unseen species, revealing identity shortcut.
risk: Species-classification-only may underperform if traits vary within species; that itself is the informative result.
alignment_with_profile: Directly operationalizes 'which signals are identifiable' by isolating species-identity as a confound, mirroring the denoising project's concern with what the objective actually learns.

title: Unseen-Clade Generalization as the Real Trait Test: Phylogenetic Leave-One-Family-Out Benchmark
motivation: Random splits leak species identity; the ecological claim requires generalization to novel clades. No prior work systematically benchmarks phylogenetic holdout for photo-based trait prediction.
hypothesis: Under leave-one-family-out evaluation, trait R^2 drops by >0.3 relative to random splits, and models trained with phylogenetic-aware augmentation recover at least half the drop.
method: Build a phylogenetically blocked benchmark (leave-one-family-out, leave-one-order-out) from iNaturalist+TRY. Add a phylogenetic-contrastive auxiliary loss that encourages morphology-based (not identity-based) features. Compare to standard training.
data: iNaturalist/GBIF images, TRY, AusTraits for clade coverage.
baseline: Random-split trait CNN; leave-one-family-out trait CNN without auxiliary loss.
metric: Delta R^2 (random minus phylogenetic split); recovery fraction from auxiliary loss.
expected_effect: Large generalization gap quantified; auxiliary loss recovers 40-60% of the gap.
risk: TRY coverage per family may be thin; mitigate with AusTraits and minimum-species thresholds.
alignment_with_profile: Frames identifiability failure as distribution shift across clades, a clean falsifiable test of what the objective makes identifiable.

title: Intraspecific Variation Is Unidentifiable: A Within-Species Prediction Ceiling Test
motivation: Species-mean labels cannot supervise within-species variation, so any claimed intraspecific prediction is untestable unless we measure the ceiling. We test whether models can predict within-species trait deviations at all.
hypothesis: Given species-mean training labels, models cannot beat a species-mean predictor on within-species trait deviations (R^2 <= 0 for deviation prediction), and this ceiling is invariant to model capacity.
method: Construct a within-species deviation task using TRY individual-level records (not means) where multiple individuals per species exist. Train models with species-mean labels and evaluate deviation prediction. Add a variance-aware loss (predict mean + species-conditional variance) and test if it helps.
data: TRY individual measurements, iNaturalist images matched to species.
metric: R^2 on within-species deviations; calibration of predicted variance.
expected_effect: Deviation R^2 near zero or negative for all models; variance-aware loss improves calibration but not point accuracy.
risk: Few species have enough individual TRY records; restrict to well-sampled species.
alignment_with_profile: Directly tests the 'unidentifiable by construction' suspicion, paralleling the denoising project's analysis of what noise/objective structure permits.

title: Objective-Identifiability Map: Contrastive vs Regression vs Reconstruction Objectives on the Same Trait Task
motivation: Different self/supervised objectives make different signals identifiable. We systematically compare which objectives recover which traits and where they fail, a direct empirical answer to the profile question.
hypothesis: Contrastive (SimCLR-style) pretraining improves unseen-species trait R^2 relative to supervised regression, while reconstruction (MAE) pretraining improves seen-species but not unseen-species performance.
method: Pretrain ResNet/ViT with (a) supervised trait regression, (b) SimCLR contrastive, (c) MAE reconstruction, (d) supervised species classification; fine-tune all on traits. Evaluate on seen/unseen species and per-trait identifiability curves.
metric: R^2 per trait, seen vs unseen species; identifiability gap.
expected_effect: Contrastive wins on unseen species by 0.05-0.15 R^2; reconstruction wins on seen species.
risk: Pretraining on limited iNaturalist subset may underfit; use subset of 1-2M images.
alignment_with_profile: Core question of the profile: which objectives make which signals identifiable, tested on a concrete ecological task.

title: Label-Noise-Aware Trait Regression: Treating Species Means as Noisy Targets
motivation: Species-mean labels are noisy estimates of individual traits; standard MSE treats them as ground truth. A noise-model-aware loss could improve generalization and reveal label-noise structure.
hypothesis: Modeling label noise as species-conditional Gaussian (variance from TRY sample size) improves unseen-species R^2 by >=0.05 over plain MSE.
method: Implement a heteroscedastic loss where target variance is estimated from TRY within-species SD and sample size. Compare to MSE and Huber. Add a noise-robustness diagnostic (inject synthetic label noise, measure degradation slope).
data: TRY with within-species SD and n; iNaturalist images.
expected_effect: Heteroscedastic loss improves unseen-species R^2 by 0.05 and flattens noise-degradation slope.
risk: TRY sample sizes may be too small to estimate variance reliably; fall back to species-level pooled variance.
alignment_with_profile: Directly transfers the 'learning signal from noisy targets' expertise from calcium imaging to trait labels.

title: Morphology-Only Counterfactual: Can Models Predict Traits From Background-Masked, Species-Agnostic Crops?
motivation: If models rely on species-identity cues (whole-plant habit, background), masking to leaf/organ crops should reveal whether morphology alone carries trait signal.
hypothesis: Models trained on organ-level crops (leaf, flower) retain >=70% of whole-image trait R^2 for leaf traits (SLA, N) but <40% for whole-plant height.
method: Use an off-the-shelf segmentation/detection model to crop leaves/flowers; train trait models on crops vs whole images. Add background randomization augmentation. Compare per-trait retention.
data: iNaturalist images, TRY; PlantTraits2024 if available.
expected_effect: Leaf traits retain most signal; height collapses, showing height is habit/identity-driven.
risk: Segmentation errors on citizen-science photos; use robust detector and manual spot-check.
alignment_with_profile: Isolates which visual signals are identifiable per trait, a clean falsifiable decomposition.

title: Trait-Identifiability Under Label Aggregation: Mean vs Median vs Quantile TRY Targets
motivation: The choice of species aggregation (mean, median, quantile) changes what the model is asked to identify. We test whether aggregation choice changes identifiability and generalization.
hypothesis: Training on species medians improves robustness to outliers and unseen-species R^2 by >=0.03 over means, while quantile targets (e.g., 90th percentile) are less identifiable (lower R^2).
method: Build parallel datasets with mean/median/quantile targets. Train identical models. Evaluate cross-aggregation transfer (train on mean, test on median) to probe what is learned.
data: TRY individual records aggregated per species; iNaturalist images.
metric: Unseen-species R^2 per aggregation; cross-aggregation transfer R^2.
expected_effect: Median target +0.03 R^2; quantile targets -0.1 R^2; cross-transfer reveals shared vs aggregation-specific signal.
risk: Aggregation differences may be small; report confidence intervals via bootstrap.
alignment_with_profile: Tests how target definition shapes identifiability, analogous to choosing denoising targets.

title: Species-Conditional Calibration: Detecting When Trait Predictions Are Just Prior Recall
motivation: A model may output the species prior mean rather than image-derived signal. We need a diagnostic that separates prior recall from visual evidence.
hypothesis: For >=50% of species, predicted trait variance across images is <20% of the species-mean prior variance, indicating prior recall dominates.
method: Define a 'prior-recall index': ratio of within-species predicted variance to between-species prior variance. Compute per species. Add an image-shuffle test (shuffle images within species; if predictions unchanged, model ignores image). Propose a fix: prior-debiasing loss that penalizes prediction-species-mean correlation.
metric: Prior-recall index distribution; image-shuffle prediction correlation.
expected_effect: High prior-recall index for many species; prior-debiasing loss reduces index and improves unseen-species R^2.
risk: Prior-debiasing may hurt seen-species accuracy; report trade-off.
alignment_with_profile: Sharp falsifiable diagnostic of identifiability failure with a concrete fix, matching the profile's analytical style.

title: Cross-Dataset Identifiability: Do Models Trained on iNaturalist Transfer to Herbarium/GBIF Specimens?
motivation: If trait prediction is real morphology reading, it should transfer across image domains (live photos vs herbarium specimens). Failure indicates domain/identity shortcuts.
hypothesis: Trait models trained on iNaturalist lose >50% R^2 when applied to herbarium specimen images, and domain-adaptation (style augmentation) recovers at least half.
method: Assemble herbarium specimen images from GBIF for overlapping species. Train on iNaturalist, test on herbarium (and vice versa). Apply style/color augmentation and a domain-adversarial loss. Measure transfer.
risk: Herbarium images may lack organs needed for some traits; restrict to leaf traits.
alignment_with_profile: Tests identifiability under domain shift, a clean falsifiable generalization test.

title: Trait-Specific Organ Attention: Which Image Regions Drive Predictions, and Do They Match Ecology?
motivation: If models attend to ecologically irrelevant regions (background, labels), predictions are not morphology-based. We test attention-ecology alignment and use it to regularize.
hypothesis: Attention maps for leaf traits overlap leaf regions significantly more than for height, and an attention-supervision loss using organ masks improves unseen-species R^2 by >=0.04.
method: Extract attention/gradient maps; compute overlap with organ segmentation masks. Train with attention-supervision (organ-mask-guided) loss. Compare to standard training on seen/unseen species.
data: iNaturalist images with organ masks (from segmentation model), TRY.
expected_effect: Leaf traits show high overlap; height low; attention supervision improves unseen-species R^2.
risk: Attention maps are noisy; use multiple attribution methods and average.
alignment_with_profile: Connects interpretability to identifiability, asking which signals the objective actually uses.

title: Few-Shot Species Adaptation: Can a Trait Model Learn a New Species From 5 Photos?
motivation: A genuine morphology model should adapt to new species with few examples; a species-recognition model cannot. This is a sharp test of what is learned.
hypothesis: Few-shot fine-tuning (5-20 images) on unseen species improves trait R^2 by >=0.1 over zero-shot, and improvement scales with morphological distinctiveness, not species frequency.
method: Meta-learn a trait model (MAML-style or simple linear probe) on seen species; evaluate few-shot adaptation on held-out species. Compare to zero-shot and to species-classification meta-learning.
metric: Few-shot R^2 gain; correlation with morphological distinctiveness (from image embeddings).
expected_effect: Trait meta-learner gains more than classification meta-learner on unseen species.
risk: Meta-learning on single GPU may be slow; use simple prototypical/linear-probe adaptation.
alignment_with_profile: Tests identifiability under data scarcity, a core question about what objectives make learnable.

title: Ensemble Disagreement as an Identifiability Probe: Where Do Models Fail and Why?
motivation: Ensemble disagreement can localize unidentifiable regions/species. We test whether disagreement predicts error and whether it correlates with species-mean label noise.
hypothesis: Ensemble disagreement correlates with absolute error (Spearman rho >= 0.4) and is higher for species with high TRY within-species SD.
method: Train an ensemble of trait CNNs with different seeds/architectures. Compute disagreement maps. Correlate with error and TRY label noise. Propose a disagreement-weighted loss and test improvement.
data: iNaturalist images, TRY with within-species SD.
metric: Spearman rho (disagreement vs error); R^2 improvement from disagreement weighting.
expected_effect: Moderate correlation; disagreement weighting improves unseen-species R^2 by 0.02-0.05.
risk: Disagreement may reflect optimization noise, not identifiability; control with architecture diversity.
alignment_with_profile: Uses uncertainty as a diagnostic of identifiability, a natural extension of the denoising project's noise analysis.

title: FloralTrait Identifiability: Predicting Flower Color/Shape From Photos and Testing Species Confounds
motivation: FloralTraits provides species-level flower traits from photos; we test whether these are visually identifiable or species-recognition artifacts, a complementary trait domain.
hypothesis: Flower color traits are highly identifiable (R^2 > 0.7) but shape/symmetry traits are largely species-identity-driven (unseen-species R^2 < 0.2).
method: Train models on FloralTraits labels; evaluate seen vs unseen species. Add color-constancy augmentation and test effect. Decompose color vs shape identifiability.
metric: Seen vs unseen-species R^2 per trait.
expected_effect: Color robust; shape collapses on unseen species.
risk: FloralTraits labels may be derived from photos already; check label provenance.
alignment_with_profile: Extends identifiability analysis to a new trait domain with a clean seen/unseen decomposition.

title: Climate-Confound Test: Are Trait Predictions Driven by Background Climate Cues?
motivation: Photos contain background/climate cues correlated with traits (e.g., arid backgrounds for high-SLA species). Models may exploit these, inflating apparent trait prediction.
hypothesis: Masking or randomizing background reduces trait R^2 by >=0.1 for at least half of traits, and climate-matched splits reduce R^2 more than random splits.
method: Apply background segmentation/masking and background swapping across climate zones. Build climate-blocked splits. Compare R^2 under random, climate-blocked, and background-masked conditions.
data: iNaturalist images with geolocation, TRY, WorldClim for climate zones.
expected_effect: Significant climate-confound effect for several traits.
risk: Background masking may remove legitimate context (e.g., height cues); report per-trait.
alignment_with_profile: Identifies a specific confound that undermines identifiability claims, with a falsifiable test.

title: Self-Supervised Denoising of Citizen-Science Photos: Does Removing Photographic Noise Improve Trait Identifiability?
motivation: Citizen-science photos contain structured noise (compression, lighting, motion). A self-supervised denoiser (Noise2Self-style) could remove nuisance variation and improve trait signal identifiability.
hypothesis: Preprocessing with a self-supervised denoiser improves unseen-species trait R^2 by >=0.03 and reduces ensemble disagreement, especially for low-quality images.
method: Train a Noise2Self/J-invariant denoiser on iNaturalist images (no clean targets). Apply as preprocessing; train trait models on denoised vs raw images. Stratify by image quality (resolution, blur).
baseline: Trait CNN on raw images; standard augmentation.
metric: Unseen-species R^2; disagreement reduction; stratified by quality.
expected_effect: Modest improvement concentrated in low-quality images.
risk: Denoiser may remove trait-relevant texture; test with and without.
alignment_with_profile: Directly reuses the self-supervised denoising expertise, testing whether noise removal aids identifiability.
